## Overview

The Kannadigas or Kannadigaru are a Dravidian ethnic group primarily native to Karnataka in southwestern India and its surrounding regions. Kannada is their principal language and belongs to the Dravidian language family. Kannada had 43.7 million native speakers in India at the time of the 2011 census, including 40.6 million in Karnataka; it is also spoken in neighbouring states and by communities in the United States, Canada, Australia, Singapore, and Malaysia. Kannada culture is associated with a long written and literary history, stone-carved temples and palaces, traditional wooden houses, music, theatre, dance, cuisine, clothing, and religious practices. Historical Kannada cultural centres include the Tungabhadra region, Hampi, Mysore, Bengaluru, the Western Ghats, and the coastal regions of Karnataka.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*Kasuti* is an embroidery work used on dresses and costumes. The source describes it as a popularly sought-after art.

*Mysore silk* is a famous form of the *Seere*, the women’s garment. The source names it.

*Ilakal Seere* is another named form of the *Seere*. The source records it as famous but gives no further information about its materials, patterns, or weaving methods.

*Khadi* is used in Kannada clothing. The source says that many people continued to use Khadi and that politicians are prominent among its wearers.

### Clothing & dress

Kannada clothing varies by place. Men’s clothing mainly includes *panche*, sometimes tied as *Kachche*, or *lungi*, whose wrapping style depends on the region. Men may also wear *Angi*, a traditional form of shirt, and a *Peta* turban in Mysuru style or Dharwad style. *Shalya* is a long piece of cloth placed over the shoulder and is commonly seen in the countryside. Khadi is also used in clothing.

Women wear *Seere*, including *Ilakal Seere* and *Mysore silk*. The draping of the Seere varies in Kodagu, North and South Karnataka, and Karavali. Young women in some parts of Karnataka traditionally wear the *Langa davani* before marriage. The source also identifies *Kasuti* embroidery on dresses and costumes. In urban settings, men’s clothing includes trousers, a shirt, and sandals, while women’s clothing includes the *shalwar*. Jeans are popular among young people, and printed Khadi or silk bearing art or an emblem is also worn.

### Architecture

Kannada architecture is associated with stone-carved sculptured palaces, temples, and traditional wooden folk houses known as *thotti mane* and *chowki mane*. Karnataka temples were commonly built from locally available stones, and their architecture includes several *shaili*, or varieties. The source highlights the musical pillars of Hampi, the monolithic statue of Gommateshvara Bahubali, the temples of Pattadakal, and the sandstone cave temples of Badami.

Named architectural centres include Hampi, Pattadakal, Badami, Aihole, Basavakalyan, Itagi, Lakkundi, Belur, Halebeedu, Shravanabelagola, Banavasi, Ikkeri, and Keladi. Itagi’s Shiva temple is described as having 68 decorated pillars, an ornate tower, and a finely worked doorway. The source also names the *Yelu Sutthina Kote* of Chitradurga, translated there as the Fort of Seven Laps.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They mention the locally available stones used in temple construction and the copper and gold coins bearing Kannada inscriptions.

They mention embroidered clothing through *Kasuti*.

## Music & performance

Kannada musical culture includes *Karnataka Shastreeya Sangeetha*, described as one of the oldest forms of music in the region. Both Hindustani and Karnataka variations are respected and nurtured by Kannadigas. Other named forms include *Bhavageete*, *Sugama Sangeetha*, *Gamaka*, *Joogera Pada*, and *Lavani*. *Yakshagana* is described as a distinctive indigenous form combining music and dance.

The *Dasa Sahitya* is Kannada literature composed by devotees in honour of Lord Vishnu or one of his avatars. *Dasa* means “servant” in Kannada and *sahitya* means literature. The Haridasas, or “servants of God,” preached Bhakti to Vishnu, and their compositions are collectively called Dasa Sahitya. Their devotional works are known as *Devaranamas*. Named examples include *Krishna Nee Begane Baaro*, *Venkatachala Nilayam*, *Jagadoddharana*, and *Tamboori Meetidava*. The Haridasas used music to spread devotional teachings and offered prayer to Vishnu through *naadopasana*.

The source names Purandara Dasa, Kanaka Dasa, Sripadaraja, Vyasatirtha, Vadirajatirtha, Jagannatha Dasa, Jayatirtha, Gopala Dasa, Vijaya Dasa, and Naraharitirtha among the composers of Dasa Sahitya. It also names Pandit Bhimsen Joshi, Gangubai Hangal, C. Aswath, Veene Doraiswamy Iyengar, Puttaraj Gawai, P. Kalinga Rao, Balappa Hukkeri, Mallikarjuna Mansur, Basavaraja Rajguru, Veene Sheshanna, T. Chowdiah, Sawai Gandharva, Kumar Gandharva, Mysore Ananthaswamy, and Mysore Manjunath among contemporary musical performers.

## Dance & theatre

Kannada theatre culture is called *Rangabhoomi*. Dramatic works include *Naataka*, plays staged in theatres or on streets, and *Bayalata*, whose name derives from *bayalu*, “open-air field,” and *ata*, “theatre.” In southern Karnataka, eastern and western varieties of Yakshagana are called Bayalata; in northern Karnataka, the name includes several other genres.

*Harikathe* is an all-night form in which one or more people tell a story with musical accompaniment. It may narrate battles, stories, devotional subjects, or *vratha* before temples on auspicious days such as Dasara and Maha Shivaratri. It combines storytelling, poetry, music, drama, dance, and philosophy.

*Togalu gombeyaata* is a form of shadow puppetry. *Gombe ata* tells stories through doll characters whose performances are controlled by people in the background using invisible threads. Named dance forms include *Dollu Kunitha*, a drum dance accompanied by singing; *Veeragase*, an energetic dance performed by jangamas; *Kamsale*, a devotional folk dance with a rhythmic instrument; *Somana Kunitha*, a ritual mask dance; *Pooja Kunita*; *Suggi Kunitha*; *Goravara Kunitha*; *Yakshagana*; *Bhootha Aradhane* or *Buta Kola*; *Gaarudi Gombe*; *Kolata*; *Huttari*; *Moodalapaya*; *Bayalata*; *Bharatanatyam*; *Jaggahalige Mela*; and *Karaga*.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used mention several festivals and ritual occasions. *Vasanta Habba*, meaning “spring festival” in Kannada, is a cultural festival organized by the Nrityagram foundation in Bengaluru. It was first held in 1990 and attracts musicians, dancers, and cultural artists from across India. *Bengaluru Habba* is a congregation of art performances in places across the city and has been celebrated every year since 2003. In 2006, the Government of Karnataka initiated *Jaanapada Jaatre*, a folklore and art event usually held on selected weekends in Lalbagh and other parts of Bengaluru.

*Dasara* and Maha Shivaratri are described as auspicious days on which Harikathe may be performed before temples. *Karaga* is celebrated annually and is dedicated to Draupadi; Bengaluru Karaga is identified as a notable event. *Jaggahalige Mela* is performed in the Hubli-Dharwad region on the occasions of Holi and Ugadi.

Harvest-related practices appear in dance traditions. *Suggi Kunitha* is performed during a harvesting festival, and the Haalakki tribe of coastal North Canara performs it during a holy harvesting festival. *Huttari* is a dance performed by Kodavas during a harvest festival.

## Foodways

Karnataka cuisine includes vegetarian and non-vegetarian dishes and reflects influences from neighbouring South Indian states and Maharashtra. *Manasollasa*, written during the reign of Kannada emperor Someshwara III, is described as one of the earliest Indian books containing chapters on culinary preparations. *Soopa Shastra* is a medieval Kannada literary work on Kannada cuisine, written in 1508 A.D.

Everyday dishes named in the source include *Bisi Bele Bath*, *Jolada rotti*, *Ragi rotti*, *Akki rotti*, *Masale rotti*, *Saaru*, *Huli*, *Benne dose*, *Ragi mudde*, *Chitranna*, *Chapathi*, *Poori*, *Avalakki*, *Puri Usli*, *Puliyogare*, and *Uppittu*. *Dosa* is linked to Udupi cuisine, and a recipe for dosa, called *dosaka*, appears in Manasollasa. Other named dishes include plain and rave *Idli*, *Masala Dosa*, *Maddur Vade*, *Neer dosa*, *Davanagere Benne dose*, and *Kadubu*. Kadubu is a rice dumpling popular in South Malnad regions such as Sakaleshpura, Mudigere, and Somwarapete, and is eaten with *huchellu* chutney.

Sweets include *Mysore Pak*, *Dharwad pedha*, *Chiroti*, *Jalebi*, *Belagavi Kunda*, *Karadantu*, *Obbattu*, *Kaayi Kadubu*, *Shenga holige*, *Thambittu*, *Karji Kai*, *Ellu unde*, *Halubai*, *Rave Unde*, and several varieties of *Payasa*. Non-vegetarian dishes include *Dhonne biriyani*, *Bamboo biriyani*, *Mutton pulao*, *Mangalore fish curry*, fish fry, *Mangalore mutton*, *chicken Sukka*, *Mandya naati style Baaduta*, *Koli saaru*, *Egg curry*, *Pork curry*, and *Boti gojju*.

## Oral tradition & literature

Kannada literature has an unbroken history of around 1500 years. Early literature was composed predominantly by Jaina court poets, and many texts from before the 12th century were religious narratives about the Jain Tīrthaṅkaras. The oldest known literary work is the *Kavirājamārga*, a work of literary criticism and poetics associated with Nṛpatuṅga Amoghavarṣa I, dated to 850 CE. It discusses meters, literary devices, and language for literary Kannada.

Pampa, Ponna, and Ranna are known as the three jewels of Old Kannada literature. Pampa’s works include *Vikramārjunavijaya* and *Ādipurāṇa*. The *Vaḍḍārādhane* by Shivakotiacharya dates to 900 CE and describes the life of Jain Acharya Bhadrabahu at Shravanabelagola. The *Kappe Arabhatta* is the oldest known existing record of Kannada poetry in tripadi metre.

The *vacana sāhitya* tradition developed with Śaiva religious, mystical, and devotional themes. Important writers include Basavanna, Allama Prabhu, and Akka Mahadevi. Later Kannada literature includes the works of Kumara Vyasa, Harihara, Rāghavaṅka, Purandara Dasa, Kanaka Dasa, Kuvempu, and others. Contemporary literature is characterized by social criticism, including the modernist Navodaya and Navya movements, the radical Dalita movement, and the progressive Bandaya.

## Language & religion

Kannada is a South Dravidian language and the official and administrative language of Karnataka. It has scheduled status in India and has been declared one of the Classical languages of India. Its history is divided into Old Kannada, or *Haḷegannaḍa*, from 450 to 1200 AD; Middle Kannada, or *Naḍugannaḍa*, from 1200 to 1700; and Modern Kannada, or *Hosagannaḍa*, from 1700 to the present.

Kannada is written in the Kannada script, which evolved from the 5th-century Kadamba script. The earliest well-attested full-length Kannada stone inscription is the Halmidi inscription, usually dated to c. 450 AD. Spoken Kannada varies regionally, with Southern, Northern, Central, and Coastal varieties. Named dialects include Mangalore Kannada, Halakki Kannada, Havigannada, Kundagannada, Nador-Kannada, Halegannada, Hatkar, Dharwad, Arebhashe, Bengaluru Kannada, and Banakal Kannada.

The sources describe Jain, Hindu, Vaishnava, Śaiva, and Vīraśaiva traditions in Kannada literary and cultural history. The Haridasas spread Bhakti to Vishnu, while the vacana tradition is associated with Śaiva and Vīraśaiva themes.
